title: Smart Scan strategy for Electronic Warfare
dataset_link: JC Wise, Radar emitter Database, 2024 huggingface.co/datasets/alan-turing institute/turing-synthetic radar dataset
description:
Development of Smart Scan Strategy for Electronic Warfare in the absence of prior reliable intelligence of emitters and their operating characteristics.
• Background Detection of hostile communication or radar signals starts with search / scan of a wide frequency spectrum which covers relevant emitters. Sensors with typically high sensitivity but with at least an order lower instantaneous bandwidth compared to overall bandwidth of the system are used to maintain surveillance over the entire spectrum. This requires a receiver / receivers to sweep over frequency bands. Hitherto strategies based on pre mission data / prior data (Open loop) are used. Usually the first priority is to rapidly sweep the entire band with the best speed possible. Open loop strategies focus only on this requirement and may lose time to nonthreatening emitters by not giving time to new or threatening ones.
• Detailed Description This problem statement focusses on development of Smart Scan Strategy for Electronic Warfare. Interception of signals is a two dimensional search problem since it involves adjusting receiver’s frequency at correct time. This includes building up figures of merit for interception performance such as probability of detection, probability of false alarm, sensitivity, Avg intercept rate, Avg Reward / cost function, percentage of correct predictions and average intercept time error. A system model for the receiver needs to be developed with measurements obtained from a simulated RF environment which has truth information on status of emitters in each band and at each time slot. The frequency spectrum for own receiver consists of many bands.
The status of environment for each frequency band at each time step can be recorded as a transmission or a non-transmission. The model should enable prediction of intercept time and interception ratio of a scanning receiver against spatially scanning and frequency agile emitters. Development of a robust scheduler using machine learning to minimize intercept time and ensure a high interception rate is the primary objective of the strategy. The model should then be trained based on hits and misses. Further, approaches to intercept a periodic scan receiver optimally should be outlined. Algorithms and techniques for the same need to be developed.
• Expected Solution Machine learning based Electronic Support receiver scheduler software
summary: Innovation (3/5): draws on machine learning applied to a clean & green technology problem, placing it in the moderate band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Clean & Green Technology. Tech Depth (3/5): centers on model. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 16/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Smart Scan Strategy for Electronic Warfare

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a smarter search strategy for detecting hostile radio and radar signals when you don't know in advance what you're looking for, one that learns to prioritize threatening or unusual signals over ones it's already identified as harmless.
overview.why_it_matters: A dumb, fixed sweep pattern wastes precious time on already-identified, non-threatening signals while new, potentially hostile emitters go undetected longer. A smarter strategy directly improves detection speed for what actually matters.
pain_points: Traditional open-loop scan strategies sweep the whole spectrum without prioritizing based on threat.
Time is lost on non-threatening, already-known emitters instead of new or threatening ones.
No prior reliable intelligence exists about emitters or their operating characteristics in the target scenario.
overview.background: Electronic warfare signal detection requires scanning a wide frequency spectrum with a narrower-bandwidth receiver, and traditional open-loop strategies don't intelligently prioritize based on threat likelihood, wasting scan time.
overview.whats_being_asked: A smart scan strategy that adaptively allocates search time based on threat likelihood, optimizing detection performance metrics (probability of detection, false alarm rate, intercept rate) without prior emitter intelligence.
expected_solution: Adaptive scan allocation prioritizing likely-threatening or unidentified emitters.
Closed-loop strategy improving on fixed open-loop sweeping.
Optimized detection performance metrics (probability of detection, false alarm, intercept rate).
Operation without reliance on pre-mission emitter intelligence.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Moderate. This is an adaptive search/resource-allocation optimization problem, a well-studied category (similar to multi-armed bandit or adaptive sensing problems), applied to a specific electronic warfare context.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Moderate. The algorithmic core (adaptive search strategy) is achievable using established optimization/reinforcement-learning approaches; the harder part is realistic simulation of the RF environment.

competitive_landscape.note: Highly specialized electronic warfare/signals intelligence PS, requires domain-specific RF/EW knowledge most teams won't have, low competition.

innovation.note: Adaptive search/allocation is an established algorithmic pattern, the value is domain-specific application to EW scanning.

invention.note: Achievable using established adaptive-search or reinforcement-learning techniques, the harder part is realistic problem simulation.

technical_feasibility.note: Real EW/RF hardware and real signal data aren't accessible, but this can be genuinely demonstrated as a simulation-based algorithm evaluation, which is realistic for 36 hours.

impact_and_benefits.note: Valuable to a specific defense operational context, a narrower, specialized audience.

architecture.note: A simulation environment plus an adaptive search algorithm, manageable complexity.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team comfortable with adaptive algorithms/reinforcement learning and willing to build a credible RF-environment simulation. Explicitly framed as an algorithmic/strategy problem, which is genuinely achievable as a simulation-based demo.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Well-defined, measurable performance metrics (probability of detection, false alarm rate, intercept rate) named directly, giving concrete evaluation criteria for your algorithm.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Without domain understanding of realistic emitter behavior patterns, your simulation environment might not reflect real EW scanning challenges meaningfully, invest research time here.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Research basic electronic warfare scanning concepts and typical emitter behavior patterns to build a genuinely meaningful simulation environment, not a generic search-optimization toy problem.

idea_0_4: Research basic EW scanning concepts and the named performance metrics (probability of detection, false alarm, intercept rate) to ground your approach.
Design your simulated RF environment: multiple simulated emitters with varying behavior patterns (some intermittent, some continuous, some more 'threatening' by simulated characteristics).
Split: one person on the simulation environment, one on the adaptive scan-strategy algorithm.
prototype_4_22: Build your simulated multi-emitter RF environment with realistic behavior variation.
Build a baseline open-loop (fixed sweep) scanning strategy for comparison.
Build your adaptive, closed-loop scan strategy that prioritizes based on emerging signal characteristics.
integration_22_30: Run both strategies against the same simulated environment and measure your named performance metrics for each.
Test with a scenario where a new, previously-unseen emitter appears mid-simulation, confirming your adaptive strategy detects it faster than the baseline.
Tune your adaptive algorithm based on these test results.
polish_30_36: Build a clear visualization comparing your adaptive strategy's performance against the open-loop baseline on the named metrics.
Rehearse explaining your algorithm's adaptive logic and why it outperforms fixed sweeping.
Prepare to discuss real-world RF environment complexities your simulation may not fully capture.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show a live simulation run where a new, previously-unseen threatening emitter appears, and your adaptive strategy detects it significantly faster than the baseline open-loop approach, that head-to-head comparison is your core evidence.

strengths: Well-defined, measurable performance metrics give concrete evaluation criteria.
Genuinely achievable as a simulation-based algorithm demonstration within 36 hours.
weaknesses: Requires domain research into realistic EW scanning behavior to build a meaningful simulation, not just a generic optimization toy problem.
Narrow, highly specialized defense audience limits broader impact appeal.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Algorithm-skill-weighted, with real domain research investment for simulation realism.
team_fit.approach: Build the baseline open-loop strategy first, it's useful both as a comparison point and ensures you have something working even if the adaptive strategy needs more tuning time.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard adaptive-search/reinforcement-learning algorithm scaffolding and simulation environment boilerplate.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing a simulated RF environment that genuinely reflects realistic EW scanning challenges (emitter behavior diversity, threat-likelihood modeling), that requires real domain research, not assumed generic search-problem setup.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-generated 'adaptive scanner' tested only against a trivial, unrealistic simulated environment would prove little about real EW scanning effectiveness, the simulation's realism is what gives the result meaning.

data_resource_availability.status: No real EW/RF signal data is accessible to a hackathon team, this is inherently a simulation-based exercise.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Build a well-researched simulated RF environment grounded in general electronic warfare scanning literature, clearly presented as a simulation-based algorithm evaluation, not claimed real-world validated performance.

judge_qna.question: How realistic is your simulated RF environment compared to actual electronic warfare scanning conditions?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Describe the specific behavior patterns and threat-modeling choices you researched and built into your simulation, and be honest about what real-world complexity (multipath, jamming, genuinely adversarial emitter behavior) isn't captured.
judge_qna.follow_up: What real EW scenario characteristic would be hardest to add to your simulation?

judge_qna.question: How does your adaptive strategy avoid being gamed by an emitter deliberately trying to appear non-threatening?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Address this directly, it's a genuine adversarial consideration in EW, describe whether and how your strategy accounts for deceptive or evasive emitter behavior, or acknowledge it as a known limitation.
judge_qna.follow_up: How would you extend your approach to handle genuinely adversarial, deceptive emitters?
